title: binary trees, recursion, and traversal patterns
concepts: A rooted tree is a connected acyclic hierarchy; in a binary tree each node has at most a left and right child, with no required ordering among values.
A subtree is itself a tree, so recursive solutions describe a node's result in terms of the results for its children and a base case for a missing node.
Preorder, inorder, and postorder depth-first traversals differ in when the current node is processed relative to its children; iterative versions use an explicit stack to simulate calls.
Level-order traversal uses a FIFO queue and processes a fixed snapshot of the queue size to separate levels.

Height and depth use different reference points: depth measures distance from the root, while height measures distance down to a deepest leaf; conventions for counting nodes versus edges must be stated.
A postorder recurrence can combine child heights or path summaries to compute properties such as maximum depth, diameter, or balance in one traversal.
Recursion depth can be proportional to tree height; a skewed tree may turn a seemingly logarithmic-depth recursion into O(n) stack usage.
Tree input representation and node identity matter: a value may repeat, null children encode structure, and comparisons of nodes may require reference identity rather than values.
